answer.exemplar: A series is absolutely convergent when the series of the absolute values of its terms converges, and conditionally convergent when the original series converges but the series of absolute values does not. The distinction matters because absolute convergence makes the sum independent of the order in which the terms are written down, whereas conditional convergence leaves the sum at the mercy of that order. Grouping a conditionally convergent series into non-adjacent blocks can therefore change its value, and a rearrangement can even push the sum to any chosen number or stop the terms from tending to zero at all. The label is therefore not bookkeeping: it tells you which manipulations of the series are safe, and a solution that regroups terms must first establish which kind of convergence is in hand.

questions.explanation: A model answer has to define both kinds by the series of absolute values and then connect the difference to a concrete consequence rather than leaving it abstract. The consequence that matters is order dependence, since an absolutely convergent series has the same sum under every permutation and every grouping while a conditionally convergent one does not, and that is the fact the later questions about grouping and rearrangement rest on.
questions.hint: Define both kinds, then say what changes about the possible rearrangements.
questions.learningObjective: explain why the two kinds of convergence behave differently

answer.exemplar: A Fourier series of a piecewise smooth function agrees with the function at every point where the function is continuous, and at a jump discontinuity it converges instead to the midpoint of the two one-sided limits, that is to their average. The value at a jump therefore carries information about the neighbourhood of the point rather than about the function at the point itself, and any statement about where a Fourier representation holds has to take this into account.

answer.exemplar: Grouping and rearranging are both ways of writing a series with its terms collected differently, but they differ in a way that decides whether the sum survives. Grouping means placing brackets around consecutive runs of terms while every term stays in its original position, so the grouped partial sums form a subsequence of the original partial sums and must approach the same limit; this holds for every convergent series, conditional or absolute. Rearranging means moving terms to new positions, so the new partial sums are not a subsequence of the old ones and the sum is no longer protected. For an absolutely convergent series the protection extends to every permutation, so rearrangement is safe there; for a conditionally convergent one it does not, and a rearrangement can change the value or stop the terms from tending to zero altogether.

questions.explanation: A model answer must separate the two operations and give the reason in each case, because the reason is what makes the conclusion stick. Grouping is protected by a subsequence argument and rearrangement is not, with the extra protection for rearrangement coming only from absolute convergence. An answer claiming rearrangement always changes the sum is as wrong as one claiming it never does.
